messages.subject: post stratification by habitat type
parts:
Hello,

I will be using a series of systematic point-transects to survey for bird=
s at airport environments. To allow for comparison with historical data =
I will be using a fixed radius of 400 m. My goal is to determine the dete=
ction probability and density for multiple species or species groups as a=
function of habitat. The environment is highly heterogeneous preventing=
a priori stratification. My concern is that if I rely upon post stratif=
ication I will be unable to estimate a detection function for proportiona=
lly smaller habitats and that the proximity of these habitats from the po=
int may bias the detection function for species observed in those habitat=
s. For example, the main habitat type is short grass so most observation=
s will be for species in that habitat type. For some points located in t=
he short grass habitat I may detect species utilitizing woodland habitats=
that are farther (say r =3D 300) from the point (r =3D 0). In contrast,=
when the point (r =3D 0) is located within woodland habitats I would exp=
ect detections to be less than 300 m, thus the data for woodland species =
observations at the short grass point might bias the detection function f=
or the entire woodland habitat. Are my concerns valid? Any guidance on t=
he appropriate analysis for data of this nature of the appropriate strati=
fication procedure would be appreciated.=20

Paige

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: post stratification by habitat type
parts:
Paige:

I agree with you that if your patches of habitat are considerably=20
smaller that the fixed radius of 400m you are using, you'll have trouble =

saying useful things about not only detectability, but also density of=20
birds within those small habitat patches. That is not a feature of=20
point transect sampling, it is simply a function of sampling at a scale=20
not appropriate for the question you are trying to answer.

If you are less interested in habitat-specific density estimates, but=20
rather more interested in overall (study area-wide) estimates of=20
density, then you can be less worried about habitat differences in=20
detectability because the property of pooling robustness will still=20
allow you to produce unbiased estimates of bird density throughout your=20
study area.
